## 1. Introduction

Intergroup contact, group membership, and minority influence are relevant to understanding prejudice and changes in social attitudes [@allport1954; @pettigrew2006; @xie2011social]. Research on changes in social conventions also motivates studying collective attitude dynamics [@centola2018experimental], although it does not establish that the same processes occur for immigration attitudes. Source-credibility research further motivates examining whether an audience's receptiveness depends on who communicates a message [@hovland1951credibility].

We use an agent-based model (ABM) to investigate how the proportion of a committed minority and prejudice discounting influence the adoption of pro-immigration attitudes among majority agents. Prejudice discounting is implemented as a reduced probability that a majority agent responds to an interaction with a committed minority speaker. This is a modelling assumption, not an empirical claim about immigrant or majority populations.

Our main outcome is the final proportion of majority agents holding an exclusively pro-immigration attitude. We also record whether adoption ever exceeds a predefined 50% threshold and the first tick when that occurs. This operational adoption threshold is **not** a claim that the model identifies a social tipping point.

## 2. The model

### Agents and attitudes

Each run starts with a fixed population. A specified proportion are committed minority agents who consistently hold a pro-immigration attitude; all other agents are non-committed majority agents who initially hold an anti-immigration attitude. These initial conditions are simplifying assumptions rather than representations of real-world demographic groups.

Majority agents can be anti-immigration, pro-immigration, or in a mixed state (`BOTH`). Mixed-state agents are not counted as fully adopting the pro-immigration position. Committed agents do not change state.

### Interactions and prejudice discounting

One simulation tick represents **one conversation between two different agents**, not a population-wide round. A speaker and hearer are randomly selected. A mixed-state speaker randomly expresses one of the two attitudes. If the speaker is committed, the hearer's update is permitted with probability `1 - prej_discount`; otherwise the prejudice-discounting mechanism does not prevent the update. The model then applies its attitude-transition rules to eligible non-committed agents. These rules represent a hypothetical opinion-dynamics process, not observed conversational behavior.

### Experimental design

The complete saved experiment uses the following settings:

| Parameter | Value |
|:--|:--|
| Total population | 1,500 agents |
| Committed minority proportion | 0.15 to 0.35, in steps of 0.05 |
| Prejudice discounting | 0 to 1, in steps of 0.1 |
| Maximum duration | 5,000 conversation ticks |
| Repetitions per combination | 100 |
| Adoption criterion | More than 50% of majority agents fully pro-immigration |
| Total simulations | 5,500 (55 combinations × 100 repetitions) |

All runs continue to the common endpoint even if an adoption threshold is crossed earlier. The output records `first_crossing_round`, `threshold_attained`, and `final_adoption` for each run. A crossing is defined strictly as a majority adoption proportion **greater than** 0.5, excluding committed minority and mixed-state agents from the adoption count.

## 3. Reproducible data loading and validation

The final 5,500 runs are stored in `data/simulation_runs.csv`. We load these saved outputs rather than rerunning the computationally intensive parameter sweep each time the report is knitted. The simulation functions and optional Shiny interface are retained in `src/simulation.R`; the analysis code is in `src/stat_analysis.R`.

```{r load-and-validate}
source("src/validation.R")
simulation_data <- read.csv("data/simulation_runs.csv")
validate_results(simulation_data)
stopifnot(nrow(simulation_data) == 5500L)
stopifnot(all(simulation_data$n_agents == 1500L))
```

The validation routine checks that essential output columns are present, adoption values are non-missing and between 0 and 1, majority state counts are valid nonnegative integers and sum to the total majority population, the threshold indicator is binary, and `final_adoption` agrees with the ratio of fully pro-immigration majority agents to all majority agents. These consistency checks **do not prove that the model's behavioural assumptions are empirically valid**.

### Optional small model smoke test

The following chunk is deliberately not evaluated when knitting. It demonstrates a quick test of the executable simulation without regenerating all 5,500 runs.

```{r optional-smoke-test, eval=FALSE}
source("src/simulation.R")
test_results <- run_sweep(
  n_agents_levels = 100,
  minority_levels = 0.25,
  prej_discount_levels = 0.5,
  n_repetitions = 2,
  max_ticks = 100,
  base_seed = 123
)
validate_results(test_results$runs)
```

## 4. Statistical analysis

We examined the average final majority adoption proportion across parameter combinations. Because this outcome is bounded between 0 and 1, the statistical analysis used a fractional logistic regression with a quasibinomial logit link. The predictors were committed minority proportion, prejudice discounting, and their interaction. The model comparison assessed whether the interaction improved fit. The associated analysis and figure-generating script is `src/stat_analysis.R`; its output can be reproduced separately from the saved CSV.

```{r summary-statistics}
library(dplyr)

descriptive_summary <- simulation_data %>%
  group_by(minority_prop, prej_discount) %>%
  summarise(
    n_runs = n(),
    mean_adoption = mean(final_adoption),
    threshold_rate = mean(threshold_attained),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

overall_adoption <- summary(simulation_data$final_adoption)
overall_adoption
```

```{r fractional-regression}
analysis_data <- simulation_data %>%
  mutate(
    minority_c = minority_prop - 0.25,
    prej_discount_c = prej_discount - 0.5
  )

model_main <- glm(
  final_adoption ~ minority_c + prej_discount_c,
  family = quasibinomial(link = "logit"),
  data = analysis_data
)

model_interaction <- glm(
  final_adoption ~ minority_c * prej_discount_c,
  family = quasibinomial(link = "logit"),
  data = analysis_data
)

summary(model_interaction)
anova(model_main, model_interaction, test = "F")
```

### Results

Across the 5,500 runs, final majority adoption ranged from approximately 0% to 41.13%, with a mean near 7.62%. A larger committed minority proportion was associated with greater adoption, whereas stronger prejudice discounting was associated with less adoption. The fractional logistic regression found a positive coefficient for minority proportion (approximately 9.31, *p* < .001), a negative coefficient for prejudice discounting (approximately −3.31, *p* < .001), and a negative interaction (approximately −1.50, *p* < .001). The interaction improved model fit, *F*(1, 5496) = 44.47, *p* < .001. The interaction suggests that the effect of minority proportion was weaker as prejudice discounting increased, on the model's logit scale.

No simulation exceeded the predefined 50% majority-adoption threshold, so threshold attainment was 0 in all 5,500 runs. Therefore, a binary logistic regression of threshold attainment and a time-to-threshold analysis were not informative. Nevertheless, final adoption proportions varied, allowing an analysis of their association with the experimental parameters.

```{r observed-adoption-heatmap, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(descriptive_summary,
       aes(x = minority_prop, y = prej_discount, fill = mean_adoption)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean final majority adoption by experimental condition",
    x = "Committed minority proportion",
    y = "Prejudice discounting",
    fill = "Adoption"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 6. Discussion and limitations

The simulated results are consistent with the idea that a larger committed minority can promote attitude change, while prejudice discounting can hinder it. Yet no condition led more than half of majority agents to adopt a fully pro-immigration attitude within 5,000 conversations. This result reflects the particular model rules, initial conditions, parameter grid, and simulation duration; it does not establish that comparable real-world attitude change is impossible.

The model simplifies immigrant and majority identities, assumes fixed committed attitudes, uses randomly selected pairwise interactions, and represents prejudice with one speaker-specific discounting parameter. Furthermore, 5,000 interactions correspond to relatively few conversations per agent on average in a population of 1,500; longer runs might produce different outcomes. Patterns in residual diagnostics also caution against treating the regression as a complete description of the data-generating process. Runs at distinct seeds are computational replications within this model, not independent samples of real people.

Future work could compare alternative interaction rules, longer time horizons, and network-based rather than uniformly random contact. The present study is a demonstration of an ABM and its sensitivity to two parameters, not an empirical estimate of immigration attitudes or a demonstrated social tipping point.
